lead.t: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways causing recurrent episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough, with variable, reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyper-responsiveness.

b: A chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways causing recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough (particularly at night or early morning).
Hallmarks : Intermittent reversible airway obstruction, chronic bronchial inflammation with eosinophils, bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperreactivity, and increased mucus secretion.
The incidence has increased significantly in Western countries over the past four decades.
The hygiene hypothesis suggests that reduced exposure to infectious organisms in early childhood may lead to defects in immune tolerance, predisposing to later hyperreactivity.
Atopic Asthma (most common)
Hallmarks: Reversible airway obstruction, eosinophilic inflammation, smooth muscle hypertrophy
Atopic Asthma: IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) driven by TH2 cells (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13)
Morphology: Curschmann spirals + Charcot-Leyden crystals in sputum

snip.t: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways causing recurrent episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough, with variable, reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyper-responsiveness.
Asthma typically shows reversible obstruction, whereas COPD obstruction is not fully reversible regardless of exposure history.
| Bronchial asthma exacerbation | Wheeze, reversible obstruction on spirometry, history of atopy; normal CXR | Predominant wheeze, rapid improvement with bronchodilators, absence of infiltrates |
Secondary spontaneous: Underlying lung disease: COPD (commonest), TB, PCP (HIV), cystic fibrosis, asthma, lung cancer, ILD, Marfan syndrome, catamenial (menstrual)

| Bronchial asthma exacerbation | Wheeze, diffuse hyper‑inflation, reversible obstruction, no unilateral findings | Bilateral wheeze, normal percussion; chest X‑ray shows hyperinflated lungs, not a visible pleural line |
Doses and stepwise plans follow GINA and BTS/SIGN; check the Kenya MoH asthma guideline and the drugs available at your facility.*
Complications: pneumonia, post-infectious cough, asthma exacerbation.
Exclude TB, bronchiectasis, cancer and asthma in a patient with chronic cough.

qs.q: A 38-year-old woman with asthma develops peripheral blood eosinophilia of 18%, p-ANCA positivity, and a new mononeuritis multiplex. CXR shows transient pulmonary infiltrates. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)
Microscopic polyangiitis
Polyarteritis nodosa
qs.e: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), also known as Churg-Strauss syndrome, is characterized by asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, p-ANCA positivity, and systemic vasculitis (which can manifest as mononeuritis multiplex and transient pulmonary infiltrates).
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - August 28, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient with asthma dies during status asthmaticus. Whorls of shed epithelium found within mucous plugs are called
o: Asteroid bodies found in mucous plugs
Curschmann spirals found in mucous plugs
Charcot-Leyden crystals found in plugs
Schaumann bodies found in mucous plugs
qs.e: Curschmann spirals are whorls of shed epithelium found in the mucous plugs of asthma. Charcot-Leyden crystals are eosinophil protein crystalloids — both are found in asthma plugs.

qs.q: The "hygiene hypothesis" in asthma suggests that
o: Poor hygiene increases bacterial colonization reducing asthma
Viral infections in childhood always prevent asthma development
Eradication of infections alters immune homeostasis promoting allergic responses
Helminth infections directly trigger bronchial hyperreactivity
qs.e: The hygiene hypothesis proposes that eradication of infections alters immune homeostasis and promotes allergic and other harmful immune responses, explaining the increased asthma incidence in Western countries.

qs.q: Which cell type is central to the pathogenesis of atopic asthma?
o: TH2 helper T cells playing the central role
TH1 helper T cells playing the central role
CD8+ cytotoxic T cells playing the central role
Natural killer cells playing the central role
qs.e: TH2 cells are central to atopic asthma. They produce IL-4 (IgE production), IL-5 (eosinophil activation), and IL-13 (mucus production), orchestrating the allergic inflammatory response.

o: Inhibits COX → shifts arachidonic acid toward leukotriene production
Directly stimulates IgE production against salicylate
Activates mast cell degranulation via IgE-independent mechanism
Blocks β2-adrenergic receptors causing bronchoconstriction
qs.e: Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway without affecting lipoxygenase, shifting arachidonic acid metabolism toward leukotriene production. Leukotrienes are potent bronchoconstrictors.

qs.q: A 28-year-old atopic male with allergic rhinitis and asthma presents with food impaction and dysphagia. Symptoms fail to improve on high-dose PPI. Endoscopic biopsies from the mid-oesophagus show dense eosinophilic infiltration superficially. What is the diagnosis?
o: GERD with peptic stricture
Gastroenteritis with eosinophilic gastritis
Achalasia — failure of LES relaxation
Eosinophilic oesophagitis — atopic background
qs.e: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune response characterised by eosinophilic infiltration of the oesophageal mucosa, often associated with atopy. It typically presents with dysphagia and food impaction and does not respond well to PPIs.

qs.q: A patient with asthma should avoid which type of medication?
o: Selective alpha-1 agonists
Non-selective beta-blockers
Selective beta-2 agonists
Selective muscarinic antagonists
qs.e: Non-selective beta-blockers (like Propranolol) can block beta-2 receptors in the lungs, leading to life-threatening bronchospasm.

es.q: A 30-year-old asthmatic patient presents to the emergency department with a severe exacerbation. Microscopic examination of their sputum may reveal characteristic findings. Name and describe two such findings associated with bronchial asthma.
es.m: 1. **Curschmann Spirals:** These are whorls of shed epithelium, typically found in mucus plugs within the airways of asthmatic patients. They represent inspissated mucus and epithelial debris. 2. **Charcot-Leyden Crystals:** These are microscopic, needle-like or diamond-shaped crystals formed from the breakdown products of eosinophil proteins. They are characteristic of eosinophil-rich inflammation, commonly seen in asthma sputum.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A sputum sample from a patient experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation reveals characteristic microscopic findings. List two such findings and briefly describe their nature.
es.m: 1. **Curschmann Spirals:** Whorls of shed epithelium, mucus, and inflammatory cells that form coiled structures within the sputum. 2. **Charcot-Leyden Crystals:** Crystalline structures formed from the breakdown products of eosinophil proteins (e.g., galectin-10), typically found in the sputum of asthmatic patients.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A 65-year-old bedridden patient with a history of asthma develops sudden dyspnea and hypoxemia. Chest imaging shows loss of lung volume in the right lower lobe. Discuss the most likely type of atelectasis and its underlying mechanism, providing two common causes specific to this patient's history. (
es.m: This presentation is most consistent with **Resorption Atelectasis**. The underlying mechanism involves obstruction of an airway, leading to the absorption of air from the distal lung parenchyma into the bloodstream, resulting in collapse. Given the patient's history, two common causes are a **mucous plug** (common in bedridden patients and asthma) or an **asthma-related bronchial obstruction** causing airway narrowing.
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

es.q: A sputum sample from a patient with severe asthma is examined. a) Identify two characteristic microscopic findings that may be present. (2 marks) b) State the key mediator responsible for eosinophil activation in asthma. (1 mark) c) Explain the mechanism by which aspirin can induce asthma. (2 marks)
es.m: a) Two characteristic microscopic findings in asthma sputum are Curschmann Spirals and Charcot-Leyden Crystals. b) IL-5 is the key mediator for eosinophil activation in asthma. c) Aspirin-induced asthma occurs due to COX inhibition, which shifts arachidonic acid metabolism towards leukotriene production.

ai.summary: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by reversible airway obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and variable symptoms including wheezing, cough, and dyspnea.

sections.p: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by reversible airway obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and variable symptoms including wheezing, cough, and dyspnea.

b: Type I Hypersensitivity: Mediated by IgE and Th2 cells.
Airway Remodeling: Chronic inflammation leads to subepithelial fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy, and mucous gland hyperplasia.
Bronchoconstriction: Triggered by allergens, cold air, exercise, or viral infections.
Symptoms: Episodic wheezing, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and nocturnal cough.
Signs: Tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, prolonged expiratory phase, and polyphonic wheezing on auscultation.
Spirometry: Demonstrates obstructive defect (FEV1/FVC < 0.70).
Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF): Diurnal variation >10%.
Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): Marker of eosinophilic inflammation.
Relievers: Short-acting beta-agonists (SABA) for acute symptom relief.
Controllers: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) to treat underlying inflammation; Long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) used in combination with ICS.
Acute Exacerbation: Oxygen, systemic corticosteroids, and nebulized bronchodilators.
Silent chest on auscultation indicates minimal air movement and impending respiratory failure.
Cyanosis and altered consciousness suggest life-threatening hypoxia and hypercapnia.
Inability to speak in full sentences or a rapid, weak pulse signal severe distress.
Pneumothorax may occur if high airway pressure causes a lung to collapse.
Status asthmaticus is a prolonged, severe attack that does not respond to standard initial treatments.

sections.p: The management goal is to reverse acute bronchospasm, reduce airway inflammation, and maintain long-term control using a stepped approach based on symptom frequency.
b: Short-acting beta-agonists (SABA) are used for immediate relief by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle during acute attacks.
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) serve as the primary long-term controller to reduce underlying airway inflammation and prevent remodeling.
Long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) are added to ICS for persistent symptoms but are never used alone due to increased mortality risk.
Oral corticosteroids are reserved for severe exacerbations to speed up recovery by suppressing the systemic inflammatory response.
Muscarinic antagonists provide additional bronchodilation if beta-agonists are insufficient or poorly tolerated by the patient.
Refer to a specialist if the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms remain uncontrolled on high-dose therapy, or life-threatening attacks occur.
Monitor peak expiratory flow rates and provide a written action plan for self-management.
Identify and avoid environmental triggers such as tobacco smoke, dust mites, and pet dander.
Assess inhaler technique at every visit to ensure medication reaches the lower airways effectively.
Encourage annual influenza vaccinations to prevent viral infections that commonly trigger severe asthma exacerbations.
COPD: Typically occurs in older smokers; characterized by fixed, non-reversible airflow limitation.
Congestive Heart Failure: 'Cardiac asthma' presents with wheeze but includes orthopnea, elevated JVP, and basal crackles.
Vocal Cord Dysfunction: Presents with inspiratory stridor rather than expiratory wheeze; confirmed by laryngoscopy.
Chest X-ray: Often normal in stable asthma; primarily used to rule out complications like pneumothorax or pneumonia.
Pulse Oximetry: Can remain normal initially in severe attacks; does not reflect the significant work of breathing or rising CO2.
Peak Flow: Highly effort-dependent; a patient may have a 'good' reading but still be in significant respiratory distress.

whenToSeekHelp: Silent chest on auscultation (minimal air movement)
Inability to complete full sentences in one breath
Cyanosis or altered level of consciousness
Peak expiratory flow rate less than 33% of predicted best
Persistent tachycardia or tachypnea despite initial bronchodilator use

faq.q: What is the hallmark physiological feature of asthma?
faq.a: Reversible airway obstruction caused by bronchial hyperresponsiveness, chronic inflammation, and smooth muscle constriction.

faq.q: Why is a 'normal' pCO2 concerning in acute severe asthma?
faq.a: It suggests respiratory muscle fatigue; early hyperventilation should typically result in low pCO2. A rising pCO2 indicates impending respiratory failure.
